## What This Page Does

This page runs the four estimators of `qte.distributional_did` on a demonstration panel, one section
per estimator, so that their output can be compared. Each section states the identifying assumption
in a paragraph and then shows the estimator at work; the assumptions are stated in full in the
reference documentation of the respective function.

All four share the same structure. For a treatment group $g$ and a period $t$ they compare a
pre-treatment period with $t$, between the treated group and a comparison group of units that are
never treated or not yet treated. Within that comparison — a _cell_ — they construct the
distribution of untreated potential outcomes for the treated group in $t$ and report quantile
treatment effects as the difference between the observed treated quantiles and those of the
counterfactual distribution. With staggered adoption there is one cell per group and period, and the
cells are aggregated to an overall effect, a per-group effect and an event-study path (compare
[Callaway & Sant'Anna 2021](#ref-cs-2021)). What the four differ in is only how they construct the
counterfactual distribution.

Every estimation returns all four aggregations at once — `res.overall`, `res.group`,
`res.event_study` and `res.group_time` — and each of them can be displayed with `plot()` or
`tabulate()`. The sections below show the overall aggregation; the header of each table repeats the
estimator, the base period and the comparison group that produced it, so that the output stays
readable on its own.

{{< include _setup-did.qmd >}}

## The Data

The demonstration data are county-level teen employment in the United States from 2003 to 2007,
together with whether a county's minimum wage was raised above the federal minimum. They are the
data used by the `did` and `qte` R packages for the same purpose, and enter `py-qte` as
`load_mpdta()`. A county is treated from the first year in which its minimum wage exceeds the
federal minimum, so the treatment groups are 2004, 2006 and 2007, and counties that never raised
their minimum wage form the comparison group.

The dataset is a demonstration device only: it has nothing to do with the estimators, it is small
enough to estimate quickly, and it has staggered adoption, which exercises the aggregation across
cells.

```{python}
#| label: lst-did-data
from qte.datasets import load_mpdta

GROUP_LABEL = (
    pl.col("group")
    .replace(float("inf"), None)
    .cast(pl.Int64)
    .cast(pl.String)
    .fill_null("never treated")
    .alias("Group")
)

# `first.treat` is 0 for counties that never raised their minimum wage; the estimators expect
# +inf for never-treated units, which is what the default of `TrtGroupConfig` assumes.
panel = load_mpdta().with_columns(
    pl.col("first.treat").replace(0, float("inf")).alias("group")
)
print(f"{panel.height:,} county-year observations for {panel['countyreal'].n_unique()} counties")
print(f"years: {panel['year'].unique().sort().to_list()}")
```

## Descriptive Statistics

The table below counts the counties by treatment group. The treated groups are very unbalanced: of
the 191 treated counties, 20 are first treated in 2004, 40 in 2006 and 131 in 2007.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-did-groups
groups = (
    panel.unique("countyreal")
    .group_by("group")
    .len()
    .sort("group")
    .with_columns(GROUP_LABEL)
    .select("Group", pl.col("len").alias("Counties"))
)
(
    GT(groups)
    .tab_header(title="Counties by first treated period")
    .fmt_number("Counties", decimals=0)
)
```

The next table reports the average log teen employment by treatment group and year. The groups
differ substantially in levels — from about 5.6 log points in the never-treated counties to about
6.5 in those first treated in 2006 — which is precisely the situation the estimators are meant to
handle: the groups need not be comparable _in levels_, only in how they would have evolved.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-did-means
means = (
    panel.pivot(on="year", index="group", values="lemp", aggregate_function="mean")
    .sort("group")
    .with_columns(GROUP_LABEL)
)
means = means.select("Group", *[c for c in means.columns if c not in ("group", "Group")])
(
    GT(means)
    .tab_header(
        title="Average log teen employment by treatment group and year",
        subtitle="Group = first year in which the county's minimum wage exceeded the federal minimum",
    )
    .fmt_number([c for c in means.columns if c != "Group"], decimals=3)
)
```

## Changes-in-Changes

Changes-in-changes ([Athey & Imbens 2006](#ref-ai-2006)) makes no assumption about the distribution
of unobservables in either group. It requires only that a single strictly increasing production
function maps unobservables into outcomes in each period, so that the comparison group's pre-to-post
quantile transformation can be applied to the treated group's pre-treatment outcomes. The
counterfactual outcome of a treated unit with pre-treatment outcome $y$ is obtained by finding the
quantile of $y$ in the pre-treatment distribution of the comparison group and reading off that
quantile from the comparison group's post-treatment distribution,

$$
k_{CIC}(y) = F^{-1}_{Y_{01}}\!\left(F_{Y_{00}}(y)\right),
$$

with $Y_{00}$ and $Y_{01}$ the comparison group's outcome before and after, and $Y_{10}$ the treated
group's outcome before. This is the least restrictive of the four on how the two groups may differ,
at the price of requiring that the distribution of unobservables within each group does not change
over time.

```{python}
#| label: lst-cic
from qte.distributional_did import estimate_changes_in_changes_effects

with timer("changes-in-changes"):
    cic = estimate_changes_in_changes_effects(
        panel,
        "lemp",
        "group",
        "year",
        "countyreal",
        qs=QS,
        bootstrap_config=BOOTSTRAP,
    )
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-cic
cic.overall.tabulate(quantiles=QS)
```

The quantile effects are identified by the mapping alone, so the only element of judgement left in
the output is the aggregation: `cic.group_time` holds the same estimate for every treatment group
and period, and `cic.event_study` aligns them by time since treatment.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cic
#| fig-cap: "Changes-in-changes: quantile treatment effects on the overall aggregation."
show_chart(cic.overall.plot())
```

## Quantile Difference-in-Differences

Quantile difference-in-differences ([Athey & Imbens 2006](#ref-ai-2006), Section 3.3) applies
difference-in-differences to every quantile instead of to the mean: the change over time of the
comparison group at the $q$-th quantile is added to the treated group's pre-treatment outcome at
that same quantile,

$$
k_{QDID}(y) = y + \left[Q_{Y_{01}}(q) - Q_{Y_{00}}(q)\right],
\qquad q = F_{Y_{10}}(y).
$$

This is justified by an additively separable model whose unobservables must be identically
distributed in all groups and periods. That is the most restrictive of the four on how the groups
may differ — the authors who formalized the estimator list it among its drawbacks — and it is what
distinguishes it from the distributional version below, which leaves the initial distributions
unrestricted.

```{python}
#| label: lst-qdid
from qte.distributional_did import estimate_quantile_did_effects

with timer("quantile difference-in-differences"):
    qdid = estimate_quantile_did_effects(
        panel,
        "lemp",
        "group",
        "year",
        "countyreal",
        qs=QS,
        bootstrap_config=BOOTSTRAP,
    )
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-qdid
qdid.overall.tabulate(quantiles=QS)
```

The effect at each quantile is the treated group's own change at that quantile net of the comparison
group's change. Because the model assumes the unobservables are identically distributed everywhere,
the two groups are effectively compared quantile by quantile, which is also why the estimator is
sensitive to the groups differing in the shape of their outcome distributions.

```{python}
#| label: fig-qdid
#| fig-cap: "Quantile difference-in-differences: quantile treatment effects on the overall aggregation."
show_chart(qdid.overall.plot())
```

## Mean Difference-in-Differences

Mean difference-in-differences is the textbook estimator. It shifts the treated group's whole
pre-treatment distribution by the change in the comparison group's mean,

$$
F_{Y(0)\mid D=1}(y) = F_{Y,\text{pre}\mid D=1}(y - \Delta),
\qquad \Delta = E[Y_{\text{post}} \mid D=0] - E[Y_{\text{pre}} \mid D=0].
$$

This implies the parallel trends assumption and therefore identifies the average effect on the
treated, but it also requires that only the location of the distribution moves. The quantile effects
it reports are consequently not evidence about how effects vary across the distribution: they are
the treated group's own distributional change net of a constant, and only the average effect rests
on the identifying assumption.

```{python}
#| label: lst-mdid
from qte.distributional_did import estimate_mean_did_effects

with timer("mean difference-in-differences"):
    mdid = estimate_mean_did_effects(
        panel,
        "lemp",
        "group",
        "year",
        "countyreal",
        qs=QS,
        bootstrap_config=BOOTSTRAP,
    )
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-mdid
mdid.overall.tabulate(quantiles=QS)
```

Only the average effect of this estimator carries identifying content. The quantile treatment
effects are the treated group's observed quantiles minus its shifted pre-treatment quantiles, so
they differ from the quantile difference-in-differences estimates above exactly by the deviation of
the comparison group's quantile change from its mean change — a property of the comparison group,
not of the treatment.

```{python}
#| label: fig-mdid
#| fig-cap: "Mean difference-in-differences: quantile treatment effects on the overall aggregation."
show_chart(mdid.overall.plot())
```

## Distributional Difference-in-Differences

Distributional difference-in-differences ([Callaway, Li & Oka 2018](#ref-clo-2018)) assumes that the
change in untreated potential outcomes has the same distribution in both groups, and that the
dependence — the copula — between that change and the initial level of untreated potential outcomes
is the same in both groups, while the initial distribution itself may differ. The counterfactual
pairs each comparison unit's own change over time with the treated pre-treatment outcome at that
unit's rank in the comparison group's pre-treatment distribution,

$$
F_{Y(0)\mid D=1}(y) =
\Pr\left\{\Delta Y_{j} + F^{-1}_{Y_{10}}\!\left(F_{Y_{00}}(Y_{j})\right) \le y \;\middle|\; D = 0\right\},
$$

where $\Delta Y_j$ is comparison unit $j$'s own change and $Y_j$ its pre-treatment outcome. This
identifies the counterfactual distribution without restricting the distribution of unobservables
across groups. Because the counterfactual is built from the comparison group's units, the
distribution of individual treatment effects is not identified, unlike for the other three.

```{python}
#| label: lst-ddid
from qte.distributional_did import estimate_distributional_did_effects

with timer("distributional difference-in-differences"):
    ddid = estimate_distributional_did_effects(
        panel,
        "lemp",
        "group",
        "year",
        "countyreal",
        qs=QS,
        bootstrap_config=BOOTSTRAP,
    )
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ddid
ddid.overall.tabulate(quantiles=QS)
```

The counterfactual is assembled from the comparison group's units, so each control unit has to be
observed in both periods of a cell; units that are not are rejected rather than silently dropped.
That also means the distribution of individual treatment effects is not identified here, unlike for
the other three, where the counterfactual is attached to the treated units.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ddid
#| fig-cap: "Distributional difference-in-differences: quantile treatment effects on the overall aggregation."
show_chart(ddid.overall.plot())
```

## Comparing the Four

The table below puts the four sets of estimates next to each other.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-did-all
#| echo: false
estimates = {
    "Changes-in-changes": cic,
    "Quantile DiD": qdid,
    "Mean DiD": mdid,
    "Distributional DiD": ddid,
}
comparison = pl.DataFrame({"Quantile": QS})
for name, result in estimates.items():
    comparison = comparison.with_columns(
        pl.Series(name, result.overall.qtt.sort("q")["effect"].to_list())
    )
(
    GT(comparison)
    .tab_header(title="Quantile treatment effects, overall aggregation, all four estimators")
    .fmt_number([c for c in comparison.columns if c != "Quantile"], decimals=3)
)
```

They do not agree. The average effects point in the same direction and are of the same order of
magnitude — between roughly $-0.02$ and $-0.05$ — but the quantile profiles differ substantially.
The widest gap is at the median, where changes-in-changes reports no effect at all and the
distributional version reports $-0.09$; at the quartiles the four are closer, between $-0.08$ and
$-0.11$ at the lower one and between $-0.02$ and $-0.05$ at the upper one.

That disagreement is the point of the exercise. The four differ only in the counterfactual
distribution they construct, so how much their estimates disagree measures how much that choice
matters in these data; with 191 treated counties spread over three small adoption groups, the
differences between the counterfactuals are large enough to make the four disagree by up to a tenth
of a log point, which is a large effect in these data. The bootstrap standard errors are not small
relative to these differences, and with 50 replications they are themselves imprecise, so read the
numbers as a demonstration of the mechanics rather than as evidence about minimum wages.

Choosing between the four is therefore not a matter of fit, which they all achieve equally by
construction, but a choice between the assumptions stated in the four sections above.
